Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-0755")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-0755")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "bf9672ec85283fdf002d83662f0b08b7", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "bf9672ec85283fdf002d83662f0b08b7", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "bf9672ec85283fdf002d83662f0b08b7", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "bf9672ec85283fdf002d83662f0b08b7", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NGINX hosts vulnerable to CVE-2026-42530 / CVE-2026-42055 (HTTP/3 UAF & HTTP/2 heap overflow) AIExploitation High
Surfaces every managed host running an NGINX build affected by the two F5-patched RCE flaws so the SOC can prioritise internet-facing instances for patching/mitigation. Article-specific because it pivots on the exact CVE IDs F5 assigned; both are unauthenticated RCE-capable on systems where ASLR is disabled or bypassable. Rationale: Keys on the two exact CVE IDs (CVE-2026-42530, CVE-2026-42055) plus the NGINX software name from the advisory; CVE-mapped TVM inventory is deterministic and the internet-facing join elevates the highest-risk hosts F5 flagged as unauthenticated-RCE exploitable. Cross-checked against: • https://my.f5.com/manage/s/article/K000161584 • https://github.com/advisories/ghsa-78jw-ww3g-9wp7 • https://www.securityweek.com/f5-patches-critical-high-severity-nginx-vulnerabilities/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/f5-issues-out-of-band-patches-for-critical-nginx-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vuln scanner reports a version string for an NGINX module/wrapper (e.g. OpenResty, Tengine) that is not actually on the affected F5 build list
  • Host running a patched build (1.30.3 / 1.31.2 / R36 P6 / 37.0.2.1) still flagged by a stale scan before re-scan
  • NGINX present only as a transitive container layer that is never network-exposed
  • Backported distro package whose version string predates the fix but already carries the vendor patch
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion !in ("1.30.3","1.31.2")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion against F5's fixed table (e.g. OSS fixed in 1.30.3/1.31.2, Plus R36 P6, NGINX Plus 37.0.2.1) and rule out backported/vendor-patched builds. 2) Contain: for unpatched internet-facing hosts apply F5's interim mitigations now — disable HTTP/3 (CVE-2026-42530); remove `ignore_invalid_headers off` or set `large_client_header_buffers` below 2MB (CVE-2026-42055) — then schedule the patch. 3) Hunt: on each affected host check NGINX error logs for worker-process crashes (pivot to the crash-loop UC) to detect any exploitation that already occurred.

NGINX worker process crash-loop — memory-corruption exploitation of CVE-2026-42530/42055 AIExploitation Medium
Detects bursts of NGINX worker-process abnormal exits (SIGSEGV/SIGABRT) or rapid worker respawns, the observable symptom of both F5 RCE flaws — a HTTP/3 QPACK use-after-free and an oversized-HTTP/2-header heap overflow that crash the worker and, with ASLR bypass, yield code execution. Article-specific because both CVEs share this exact failure mode (worker restart) per F5's advisory. Rationale: Both CVEs' confirmed effect (per F5 + GitHub advisory) is an NGINX worker-process restart from heap/UAF corruption; SIGSEGV/SIGABRT crash-bursts and abnormal worker respawn rate are the highest-fidelity host signal of attempted exploitation when no payload IOCs exist. Cross-checked against: • https://my.f5.com/manage/s/article/K000161584 • https://github.com/advisories/ghsa-78jw-ww3g-9wp7 • https://securityaffairs.com/193842/security/f5-patches-critical-nginx-vulnerabilities-enabling-unauthenticated-code-execution.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1499.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OOM-killer terminating nginx workers under memory pressure (signal 9, not 11/6 — already excluded, but mixed log formats can leak)
  • Buggy third-party NGINX module crashing workers unrelated to these CVEs
  • Planned config reload / logrotate spawning fresh workers (SIGHUP, not a crash signal)
  • Blue/green deploy or container restart cycling many nginx workers in a short window
  • Disk-full or upstream-timeout storms causing repeated worker recycling
Suppression filter
| where SampleMessage !has "signal 9" and SampleMessage !has "gracefully shutting down" and SampleMessage !has "signal 1"
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the host's nginx error_log around the crash window; confirm SIGSEGV/SIGABRT (memory corruption) vs SIGKILL/OOM, and check the running NGINX version against the patched list plus whether HTTP/3 or HTTP/2-proxy+grpc_pass is enabled. 2) Contain: if unpatched and internet-facing, apply F5 mitigations immediately (disable HTTP/3; remove `ignore_invalid_headers off` or drop `large_client_header_buffers` below 2MB) and isolate/patch the host. 3) Hunt: correlate access/QUIC logs for the source IP sending oversized HTTP/2 headers (>2MB) or malformed HTTP/3 QPACK sessions just before each crash, and check for any non-nginx child process spawned by nginx (sign of successful RCE post-ASLR-bypass).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where FileName == "nginx" and InitiatingProcessFileName == "nginx"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "worker process"
| summarize WorkerSpawns = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SampleCmd = any(ProcessCommandLine) by DeviceId, DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where WorkerSpawns >= 10   // healthy nginx rarely recycles workers; >=10 respawns / 10m = crash loop (baseline ~0)
| sort by LastSeen desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ProcessName == "nginx" or SyslogMessage has "nginx"
| where SyslogMessage has "exited on signal"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("signal 11","signal 6","SIGSEGV","SIGABRT","core dumped")
| summarize CrashCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleMessage = any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where CrashCount >= 3   // 3+ SIGSEGV/SIGABRT worker exits in 10m far exceeds normal (0)
| sort by LastSeen desc
source:linux.syslog @process.name:nginx "exited on signal" ("signal 11" OR "signal 6" OR SIGSEGV OR SIGABRT)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/nginx$/i ParentBaseFileName=/nginx/i
| regex("worker process", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count(as=WorkerSpawns))
| WorkerSpawns >= 10

Chromium subprocess-launcher switch + --no-zygote co-occurrence (Crawl4AI extra_args RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts a single Chromium/headless-shell process whose command line carries --no-zygote together with a subprocess-launcher override (--utility-cmd-prefix / --renderer-cmd-prefix / --gpu-launcher / --browser-subprocess-path). This tuple is the execution signature of GHSA-r253-r9jw-qg44, where attacker-supplied browser_config.extra_args forces Chromium to fork/exec an arbitrary command. The combination is near-pathognomonic — legitimate Crawl4AI never sets a launcher-override prefix. Rationale: Uses the exact launcher-override switches named in the advisory (--utility-cmd-prefix/--renderer-cmd-prefix/--gpu-launcher/--browser-subprocess-path) gated on --no-zygote; per the Chromium zygote docs this combo is what forces a fresh fork/exec of the injected command, making it high-fidelity. Chromium switches are always lowercase canonical so no Datadog casing variants are needed. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/GHSA-r253-r9jw-qg44/ • https://github.com/chromium/chromium/blob/main/docs/linux/zygote.md
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer debugging Chromium under valgrind/gdb using --renderer-cmd-prefix on a workstation
  • CEF/Electron app that sets --no-zygote for stability but never sets a launcher prefix (won't match — requires both)
  • Automated browser-performance testing harness intentionally wrapping subprocesses
  • Crash-reproduction tooling that prefixes the GPU process launcher
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("valgrind","gdb","--enable-logging=stderr") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bash","sh","make","ctest"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and read the value after the launcher switch — that string IS the attacker command; capture the parent (Crawl4AI/uvicorn/python) and the runtime user. 2) Contain: kill the Chromium process tree, isolate/stop the Crawl4AI container, and rotate any secrets/tokens mounted into it (env, mounted files) since RCE ran as the runtime user. 3) Hunt: confirm the package is <=0.8.9, search for child processes the browser spawned (UC2), and review WAF/proxy logs for the POST /crawl* that delivered the payload (UC3).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine contains "--no-zygote"
| where ProcessCommandLine contains "--utility-cmd-prefix"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "--renderer-cmd-prefix"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "--gpu-launcher"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "--browser-subprocess-path"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine contains "--no-zygote"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine contains "--utility-cmd-prefix"
    or ActingProcessCommandLine contains "--renderer-cmd-prefix"
    or ActingProcessCommandLine contains "--gpu-launcher"
    or ActingProcessCommandLine contains "--browser-subprocess-path"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects a Chromium/headless process launched with --no-zygote together with a subprocess-launcher override switch, the execution signature of GHSA-r253-r9jw-qg44 argument-injection RCE in Crawl4AI.
references:

Headless Chromium spawning shell/interpreter child (Crawl4AI injected-command exec) AIExploitation High
Hunts a browser process (chrome/chromium/headless_shell) that forks a shell, network tool or scripting interpreter as a direct child. In normal operation Chromium only spawns more Chromium/crashpad processes; a /bin/sh, curl, python or nc child is the post-exploitation result of the extra_args launcher-prefix injection executing the attacker command as the container runtime user. Rationale: Pivots on the parent→child relationship the advisory describes ('causing Chromium to fork/exec an attacker-controlled command'); in a Crawl4AI container the browser legitimately only spawns more browser/crashpad processes, so a shell/curl/python child is high-fidelity. Datadog left empty because the standard linux.auditd schema exposes no parent-process field to anchor the chain. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/GHSA-r253-r9jw-qg44/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom crawler post-processing that legitimately pipes browser output through python/node
  • Container healthcheck scripts mis-parented under the browser during teardown
  • Debug builds invoking curl/wget from a browser test harness
  • Sandbox-disabled CI runs where the browser wrapper is a shell script
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("healthcheck","/usr/local/bin/entrypoint") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the child ProcessCommandLine and any network destination it contacted; identify the runtime user and whether the child reached out-of-band (curl/wget/nc to an external IP). 2) Contain: terminate the child + Chromium tree, stop/quarantine the container, and block the egress destination at the firewall; rotate mounted secrets and tokens. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC1 (launcher-switch cmdline) on the same host/time, review FileWritten events by the child for dropped payloads, and check DeviceNetworkEvents for follow-on C2 from the runtime user.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome","chromium","chromium-browser","headless_shell","chrome-headless-shell","chrome.exe","chromium.exe","headless_shell.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","curl","wget","python","python3","nc","ncat","netcat","perl","ruby","node")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("chrome","chromium","chromium-browser","headless_shell","chrome-headless-shell")
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","curl","wget","python","python3","nc","ncat","perl","ruby","node")

Crawl4AI path-traversal: crawler Python process writes to RCE-enabling paths (cron.d, authorized_keys, shell rc, site-packages) AIInstallation High
Hunts the exploitation primitive of GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3: the crawl4ai download sink (HTTP Content-Disposition filename or Playwright suggested_filename) escaping the downloads directory and writing attacker-controlled bytes to one of the four RCE sinks the advisory names. A web-crawler Python process should never write to /etc/cron.d, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, shell rc files, or the Python import path, making this high-fidelity for the file-write-to-RCE escalation. Rationale: Uses the four RCE sinks the advisory explicitly names (/etc/cron.d/evil, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, shell rc-file, Python module on import path) keyed to a python initiating process, the only attacker-influenced behaviour this file-write-to-RCE bug produces. Cross-checked the GHSA, GitLab GLAD (CWE-22+CWE-59, fix 0.9.0) and VulnCheck's related crawl4ai Docker advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3/ • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/crawl4ai-docker-api-local-file-inclusion-via-file-url-handling
ATT&CKT1190 T1053.003 T1098.004 T1546.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • pip/pip3 or poetry installing or upgrading a package writes legitimately into site-packages/dist-packages during a deploy of the crawler container
  • A maintenance/config-management Python script (Ansible/SaltStack module run via python) legitimately writing a cron job under /etc/cron.d
  • Developer running `python -m venv` or editable installs touching site-packages on a build host
  • Legitimate crawl4ai self-update writing its own package files
  • An ops automation Python tool rotating a service account's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pip","pip3","poetry","uv") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","-m pip","setup.py","python -m venv")) and FolderPath has_any ("/site-packages/","/dist-packages/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine and FolderPath/FileName — confirm the writer is the crawl4ai service (uvicorn/gunicorn/python crawler) and not pip/deploy tooling, and inspect the written file's content (cron line, SSH key, rc payload). Check the SHA256 and the source URL/Content-Disposition that triggered the download. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the crawler process, remove the dropped file, and rotate any exposed SSH keys/service creds; confirm crawl4ai is upgraded to >=0.9.0 and CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN auth is enabled. 3) Hunt: enumerate all files written by that python PID outside the downloads dir, review web/proxy logs for unauthenticated POSTs to the Docker /crawl endpoint with HTTPCrawlerConfig, and run UC2 to confirm whether cron/sshd executed the dropped payload.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "python" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "crawl4ai"
| where (FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron.d","/etc/cron.daily","/etc/cron.hourly","/var/spool/cron","/site-packages/","/dist-packages/"))
    or FileName =~ "authorized_keys"
    or FileName in~ (".bashrc",".bash_profile",".profile",".zshrc",".bash_login")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "python" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "crawl4ai"
| where (TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/cron.d","/etc/cron.daily","/etc/cron.hourly","/var/spool/cron","/site-packages/","/dist-packages/"))
    or TargetFileName =~ "authorized_keys"
    or TargetFileName in~ (".bashrc",".bash_profile",".profile",".zshrc",".bash_login")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI RCE confirmation: cron/sshd/shell executes payload dropped by crawler within correlation window AIActions on Objectives Medium
Second-stage confirmation for GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3: after the crawl4ai Python process writes to /etc/cron.d or ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, this correlates a subsequent process spawned by cron/crond/sshd (or a shell sourcing a modified rc) on the same host within 24h — evidence the arbitrary write actually escalated to code execution. Distinct pivot from UC1: process-execution telemetry joined to the file-write event, not the write alone. Rationale: Chains the UC1 drop (python writing /etc/cron.d or authorized_keys) to a cron/sshd-spawned execution on the same host inside 24h, confirming the advisory's stated escalation path (cron entry / authorized_keys -> RCE) actually fired rather than just the write attempt. Surfaces requests asserting auth-user: service-brother that target sensitive routes (/admin, /protected, /graphql, /internal) or use mutating methods (POST/PUT/DELETE/PATCH) — i.e. the validateToken() bypass actually being used to act on protected resources rather than merely probed. Baseline legitimate service-brother destinations/methods and treat deviations as exploitation. Rationale: Combines the article's bypass marker (service-brother) with sensitive routes named in the fix (consumers: rest, graphql) and the example endpoint (/protected); mutating methods + 2xx on protected paths is the 'bypass was used' signal (reviewer #2/#4). The Splunk Web-datamodel half is the access-pattern net since CIM Web does not model request headers — confirm the header in WAF logs. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@acastellon/auth/GHSA-gfj5-979r-92pw/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-GFJ5-979R-92PW

1) Triage: for each hit, confirm the request both asserts service-brother AND came from outside the service mesh; check the HTTP status — a 2xx on an admin/mutating route means the bypass succeeded. Diff the destination/method against the service-brother baseline. 2) Contain: revoke/rotate any secrets or data the route could expose, block the source, and enforce mTLS (TRUSTED_MTLS_SERVICES allowlist) so header-only identity is rejected. 3) Hunt: reconstruct the full session from that source across all routes, look for data exfil or further writes, and check downstream services that trusted the forwarded identity.

Vulnerable @acastellon/auth (<2.3.0) package present on host AIExploitation Medium
Inventory hunt for the affected npm package on disk — node_modules\@acastellon\auth\auth.js / package.json — which contains the spoofable validateToken() bypass below v2.3.0. Identifies servers running the vulnerable dependency so they can be patched before the header bypass is exploited; analyst confirms the exact version (2.2.0 vulnerable, fixed in 2.3.0+) from the package.json. Rationale: Targets the article's exact affected package and source file (auth.js) at the canonical npm scoped path; presence below v2.3.0 is the vulnerable surface for the bypass. This is the one detection expressible on endpoint/file telemetry since the header bypass itself is invisible to EDR. netlicensing-mcp get_product called with path-traversal product_number (../token) AIExploitation High
Hunts MCP/application-log evidence of the netlicensing_get_product tool being invoked with a product_number containing path-traversal sequences (../, %2e%2e, %2f, %5c). This is the raw attacker input for GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8, captured before httpx normalizes /product/../token into /token. Rationale: Uses the exact MCP tool name (netlicensing_get_product) plus the article's documented traversal payloads (../token and the encoded variants %2e%2e/%2f/%5c the remediation adds regression tests for). A Product-fetch tool receiving path separators in its identifier argument has no legitimate use. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch empty: the payload is an in-process MCP tool argument, not a Windows process command line or AWS API call. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/netlicensing-mcp/GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8/ • https://netlicensing.io/wiki/restful-api • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team running the published PoC / regression tests against a non-production MCP instance
  • DAST/WAF vulnerability scanner probing the MCP server with traversal fuzz strings
  • Developer pasting an encoded URL fragment as a product number by copy-paste error
  • Internal red-team validation of the GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8 patch
Suppression filter
| where not (SyslogMessage has_any ("regression-test", "pytest", "VULN-001", "scanner"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full log line — confirm the tool is netlicensing_get_product and the product_number literally contains ../ , %2e%2e, %2f or %5c. Identify the MCP client identity / API key that made the call. 2) CONTAIN: If product is < 0.1.8, treat as confirmed exploit — rotate the NetLicensing API key the MCP server holds, and any APIKEY tokens (especially ROLE_APIKEY_ADMIN) that could have been disclosed; upgrade to >=0.1.8. 3) HUNT: Search the same source for other tool calls from this client and for get_product responses containing tokenType/APIKEY (UC3) to confirm whether a key was actually returned.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "netlicensing_get_product"
| where SyslogMessage contains "../" or SyslogMessage contains "..\\" or SyslogMessage contains "%2e%2e" or SyslogMessage contains "%2f" or SyslogMessage contains "%5c"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, HostName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog netlicensing_get_product AND ("../" OR "%2e%2e" OR "%2f" OR "%5c")
APPLICATION
index=* "netlicensing_get_product" ("../" OR "..\\" OR "%2e%2e" OR "%2f" OR "%5c")
| table _time host source _raw
| sort - _time
NetLicensing REST request URL containing both /product/ and traversal-to-token (wire signature) AIExploitation High
Hunts forward-proxy / SWG logs for a single request to go.netlicensing.io (or backup netlicensing.labs64.com) whose URL contains the /product/ segment together with /token or an encoded traversal sequence — the on-the-wire artefact when the percent-encoded GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8 payload survives httpx normalization. Legitimate traffic hits /product OR /token, never both in one URL. Rationale: Anchors on the confirmed REST base host go.netlicensing.io (+backup netlicensing.labs64.com) and the structural impossibility of a legitimate URL containing both /product/ and a token/traversal segment. Targets the encoded variants (%2e%2e/%2f/%5c) that survive WHATWG normalization to the wire. Datadog empty: no web-proxy source in this tenant's source list; Defender/Falcon empty: no HTTP path visibility inside HTTPS to a SaaS endpoint. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/netlicensing-mcp/GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8/ • https://netlicensing.io/wiki/restful-api
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WAF/DAST scanner traversal fuzzing of the NetLicensing integration
  • Authorized pentest validating the GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8 fix
  • A proxy that pre-normalizes URLs and rewrites %2e%2e (would suppress, not false-positive)
  • Manual cURL testing by an engineer reproducing the advisory
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the proxy log shows a single request to go.netlicensing.io with /product/ + token/traversal in the URL; identify the SourceIP (the MCP server host) and any authenticated SourceUserName. 2) CONTAIN: Block/inspect the source if unauthorized; rotate the NetLicensing API key the MCP server uses and any potentially-exposed APIKEY tokens; ensure the package is upgraded to >=0.1.8. 3) HUNT: Pivot to MCP/app logs (UC1) for the originating get_product call and to UC4 for bare /token hits from the same host that the literal ../ form would have produced.

netlicensing-mcp get_product response leaking APIKEY/token fields (redaction bypass) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts MCP/application logs for a netlicensing_get_product (Product-typed) tool call whose output contains token-specific fields — tokenType APIKEY, ROLE_APIKEY_ADMIN, or a console_url under /#/tokens/. Per GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8 these are exactly the fields redact_token_read() would mask; a Product tool returning them is direct evidence the traversal reached /token and leaked a plaintext key. Rationale: Pairs the Product tool name with the exact token-leak markers from the advisory's PoC output (tokenType=APIKEY, role ROLE_APIKEY_ADMIN, console_url https://ui.netlicensing.io/#/tokens/<key>). The legitimate token tools (get_token/list_tokens) may emit these too, but a PRODUCT tool emitting them is unambiguous bypass evidence. Hunting tier because it depends on the deployment logging tool responses. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch empty: app-layer response content unavailable to those platforms. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/netlicensing-mcp/GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8
ATT&CKT1212 T1552
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Verbose debug logging that echoes a legitimate get_token response near a get_product log line (correlation artefact)
  • Replay of the published PoC output in a test/log-sample dataset
  • A custom downstream tool that legitimately enriches product data with token metadata (rare; should be validated)
  • Log aggregation that interleaves get_product and get_token messages making string co-occurrence appear in one record
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the record is a get_product RESPONSE (not a get_token call) carrying a real (unmasked) APIKEY number/console_url. Note the MCP client identity and the leaked token's role. 2) CONTAIN: Immediately revoke/rotate the disclosed APIKEY token — if ROLE_APIKEY_ADMIN, treat the entire NetLicensing account as compromised (full read/write/delete) and rotate the account owner credential; upgrade to >=0.1.8. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all get_product calls from this client (UC1) to scope which keys were exfiltrated, and review NetLicensing audit/console activity for use of the leaked admin token.

| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, HostName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

First-seen access to NetLicensing /token REST endpoint from MCP egress source AIActions on Objectives Medium
Behavioral baseline over proxy logs: flags a source host issuing GET /core/v2/rest/token to go.netlicensing.io when that source has no prior history of token-endpoint access in the baseline window. This covers the GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8 case where the literal ../token payload is normalized by httpx to a bare /token request that carries no traversal artefact on the wire. Rationale: Catches the literal ../token variant that UC2 misses (httpx collapses /product/../token to a bare /token GET). Because the dedicated token tools also legitimately hit /token, this relies on a 14-day per-source baseline so only newly-token-active sources surface — Medium confidence by design. Anchored on the confirmed REST path /core/v2/rest/token. Datadog empty (no proxy source in tenant list); Defender/Falcon empty (no HTTPS path visibility). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/netlicensing-mcp/GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8/ • https://netlicensing.io/wiki/restful-api

Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A host legitimately beginning to use netlicensing_get_token / list_tokens for the first time (benign new token-tool adoption)
  • New MCP server instance deployed in the baseline-free window
  • Proxy NAT change re-mapping an existing token-user to a new SourceIP
  • Scheduled token-rotation job running from a host added recently

| where SourceIP !in ("")  // populate with confirmed-benign MCP/token-tool egress IPs after first triage to suppress benign new-adopter sources
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Determine whether the new source's /token access correlates with a get_product call in MCP/app logs (UC1/UC3). If the source is the MCP server host and no legitimate token tool was invoked, treat as the normalized traversal. 2) CONTAIN: Rotate any APIKEY tokens the source could have read; confirm package >=0.1.8. 3) HUNT: Add confirmed-benign token-using sources to an allowlist, then widen the window to look for repeated first-seen token access across other hosts.
let lookback = 14d;

    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(lookback) .. ago(1d))
    | where DestinationHostName has_any ("go.netlicensing.io","netlicensing.labs64.com")
    | where RequestURL contains "/core/v2/rest/token"
    | summarize by SourceIP;

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Explorer spawning script host (wscript/cscript/mshta) — USB LNK worm initial execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — USB worm spreads crypto-stealing malware via Windows shortcut files
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] PowerShell adding Defender scan exclusions (crypto-clipper worm staging) · [LLM] Scheduled task created by script host (crypto-clipper stealer/USB-monitor persistence) · [LLM] Bulk .lnk creation replacing documents by a script host (crypto-clipper worm masquerade) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ugate.exe renamed Tor binary execution (crypto-clipper C2 tunnel) · [LLM] Non-browser process connecting to local Tor SOCKS proxy 127.0.0.1:9050 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Script host executing payload file named 'cfile' (crypto-clipper C2 EVAL RCE) · [LLM] curl spawned by script host exfiltrating over Tor SOCKS (crypto-clipper screenshot upload)
Explorer spawning script host (wscript/cscript/mshta) — USB LNK worm initial execution AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the CryptoBandits/crypto-clipper USB worm's entry point: a user double-clicks a malicious .lnk that masquerades as a document, and explorer.exe launches a Windows script host instead of an Office app. Normal document opens spawn winword/excel/acrord32 — a script host child of explorer is the worm's tell. Rationale: Microsoft's writeup and the BleepingComputer article both state infection begins by opening a .lnk on USB that replaces real documents; the diagram confirms the LNK invokes wscript/cscript. Explorer→script-host is the article-specific anomaly (real docs open Office apps). Cross-checked the Microsoft Security Blog and The Hacker News. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/microsoft-details-windows-clipper.html • https://cyberinsider.com/microsoft-warns-of-usb-worm-like-malware-using-tor-for-stealth/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1091
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy .hta/.vbs desktop shortcuts for internal apps
  • Admin who keeps a .vbs maintenance script on the desktop
  • Software that registers .wsf handlers and is launched from a shortcut
  • Citrix/Kiosk launchers that shell out via wscript from explorer
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("\\Program Files\\", "\\Windows\\System32\\") and FolderPath has "\\Windows\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the script host's child cmdline and FolderPath — confirm the script/target lives on a removable drive (D:-Z:) or a freshly written staging folder, and whether the originating .lnk sits next to a same-named hidden document. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the wscript/cscript tree, and quarantine the source USB; block ugate.exe and 127.0.0.1:9050 egress via EDR. 3) Hunt: on the same host pivot to DeviceFileEvents for bulk .lnk creation in Documents/Desktop/Downloads, schtasks /create by the script host, and Add-MpPreference exclusion calls (UCs in this set).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Child = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\explorer.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\cscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Explorer Spawning Windows Script Host (USB LNK Crypto-Clipper Worm)
id: a3f1c2d4-5b6e-4a7c-8d9e-0f1a2b3c4d5e
status: experimental
description: Detects explorer.exe launching wscript/cscript/mshta, the execution shape of the crypto-clipper USB worm's document-masquerading LNK files.
references:

  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/explorer\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/(wscript|cscript|mshta)\.exe$/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="explorer.exe" AND Processes.process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe") AND NOT Processes.user IN ("*$") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
PowerShell adding Defender scan exclusions (crypto-clipper worm staging) AIInstallation High
The worm runs PowerShell to exclude its staging folders and the Windows binaries it abuses (wscript/cscript/curl/schtasks) from Defender scanning before dropping payloads. Hunts Add-MpPreference/Set-MpPreference exclusion or real-time-protection tampering. Rationale: Decoded from the article's execution-flow diagram (step 2: 'Worm runs PowerShell to exclude staging folders and Windows binaries used in execution from getting scanned'). Add-MpPreference exclusion of attacker tooling is high-fidelity defense-evasion. Corroborated against the Microsoft blog and image https://www.bleepstatic.com/images/news/u/1220909/2026/June/executionflow.jpg. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/ • https://www.bleepstatic.com/images/news/u/1220909/2026/June/executionflow.jpg
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • EDR/AV onboarding or migration scripts setting exclusions
  • Backup/EDR vendor installers excluding their own folders
  • Developers excluding build/output directories for performance
  • SCCM/Intune compliance baselines configuring Defender
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ccmexec.exe","sense.exe","setup.exe","msiexec.exe") and ProcessCommandLine !has "Program Files\\Windows Defender"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the exact exclusion path/process added — worm exclusions point at user-writable staging dirs (AppData/Temp/Public) or at wscript/cscript/curl/schtasks rather than vendor product folders. Check the initiating user and whether it was admin-approved. 2) Contain: remove the exclusion (Remove-MpPreference), isolate the host, and run a full scan now that exclusions are gone. 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts where the same exclusion path/process was added in the last 30 days; pivot to UCs for explorer→scripthost, ugate.exe, and localhost:9050.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Add-MpPreference","Set-MpPreference")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ExclusionPath","ExclusionProcess","ExclusionExtension","DisableRealtimeMonitoring")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("Add-MpPreference","Set-MpPreference")
| where CommandLine has_any ("ExclusionPath","ExclusionProcess","ExclusionExtension","DisableRealtimeMonitoring")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Defender Exclusion or Real-Time-Protection Tampering via PowerShell (Crypto-Clipper Worm Staging)
id: b4e2d3c5-6c7f-4b8d-9e0f-1a2b3c4d5e6f
status: experimental
description: Detects Add-MpPreference/Set-MpPreference adding scan exclusions or disabling real-time monitoring, the staging step the crypto-clipper USB worm performs before dropping payloads.
references:

Scheduled task created by script host (crypto-clipper stealer/USB-monitor persistence) AIInstallation Medium
The worm creates scheduled tasks — including the stealer task that re-launches wscript/cscript from disk, and a task that watches for newly connected USB drives. Hunts schtasks.exe /create spawned by a script host or registering a script-host action. Rationale: Article: 'The worm creates a scheduled task that monitors for newly connected USB storage devices'; diagram step 5 confirms the task 'invokes the stealer payload (wscript/cscript) from disk.' A schtasks /create with a script-host parent/action is article-specific persistence. Corroborated against Microsoft blog + decoded diagram. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/microsoft-details-windows-clipper.html
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • GPO/login scripts registering maintenance tasks via cscript
  • Software installers wrapping schtasks in a VBScript
  • Backup tools scheduling jobs through PowerShell
  • IT automation (PDQ/PSAppDeployToolkit) creating tasks
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "\\Windows\\CCM\\" and ProcessCommandLine !has "\\Program Files\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the created task's action (/tr) and trigger — worm tasks point at a wscript/cscript invoking an on-disk script with args and may use an event/USB-insertion trigger; capture the script path. 2) Contain: delete the task (schtasks /delete), isolate host, quarantine the referenced script and any USB source. 3) Hunt: query other hosts for the same task name/action; pivot to ugate.exe execution and localhost:9050 connections to confirm stealer activation.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create" or ProcessCommandLine has "-create"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe")
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("wscript","cscript",".js",".vbs")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create"
| where (ParentProcessName endswith "\\wscript.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\cscript.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe")
    or CommandLine has_any ("wscript","cscript",".js",".vbs")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: schtasks /create Spawned by Windows Script Host (Crypto-Clipper Worm Persistence)

Bulk .lnk creation replacing documents by a script host (crypto-clipper worm masquerade) AIInstallation High
The worm hides original .doc/.xlsx/.pdf files and drops same-named .lnk shortcuts in their place so opening a 'document' runs the malware. Hunts a single script-host process writing many .lnk files into user document/desktop/download folders in a short window. Rationale: Article: 'the malware hides the originals and replaces them with malicious shortcuts bearing the same names.' Bulk same-window .lnk drops by a script host into doc folders is a distinctive, low-FP file-event pivot (threshold detection, so no single-event Sigma). Microsoft confirms targeting .doc/.xlsx/.pdf. Corroborated via Microsoft blog and The Hacker News. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/microsoft-details-windows-clipper.html
ATT&CKT1564.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup/sync tools (OneDrive/Dropbox) generating shortcut stubs
  • Software installer placing multiple Start-menu/desktop shortcuts via a setup script
  • Roaming-profile or folder-redirection logon scripts rebuilding shortcuts
  • Admin migration script recreating document shortcuts
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("onedrive.exe","explorer.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "\\Program Files\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm each new .lnk sits beside a now-hidden same-named .doc/.xlsx/.pdf and that the .lnk target invokes wscript/cscript — open one .lnk's target string. 2) Contain: isolate the host, stop the writing process tree, and restore/unhide the original documents from the same folders; quarantine the source USB. 3) Hunt: sweep file shares and other endpoints for the same .lnk-beside-hidden-doc pattern (worm spreads to network/removable drives); correlate with schtasks USB-monitor task creation.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".lnk"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Documents", @"\Desktop", @"\Downloads")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe")
| summarize LnkCount = dcount(FolderPath), Sample = make_set(FolderPath, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where LnkCount >= 5   // worm bulk-replaces documents; benign script-driven .lnk creation is rarely 5+ at once
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileRename")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".lnk"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Documents", @"\Desktop", @"\Downloads")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe")
| summarize LnkCount = dcount(TargetFilePath), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated)
    by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where LnkCount >= 5
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*.lnk OR *.LNK) @TargetFilename:(*\\Documents\\* OR *\\Desktop\\* OR *\\Downloads\\*) @Image:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\mshta.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/(wscript|cscript|powershell|cmd|mshta)\.exe$/i | regex("(?i)\.lnk$", field=TargetFileName) | regex("(?i)(Documents|Desktop|Downloads)", field=TargetFileName) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(as=lnkCount)) | lnkCount >= 5
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` dc(Filesystem.file_path) as LnkCount min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action="created" AND Filesystem.file_name="*.lnk" AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Documents\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Desktop\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Downloads\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_id _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where LnkCount >= 5 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(Filesystem.file_path) as LnkCount min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action="created" AND Filesystem.file_name="*.lnk" AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Documents\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Desktop\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Downloads\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_id _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where LnkCount >= 5 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
ugate.exe renamed Tor binary execution (crypto-clipper C2 tunnel) AICommand & Control High
The stealer launches a renamed Tor executable named ugate.exe in a hidden window to tunnel C2 over an .onion hidden service. Hunts execution of ugate.exe and, more broadly, any process whose original filename is tor.exe but runs under a different name. Rationale: Both BleepingComputer and Microsoft name the Tor executable ugate.exe; the diagram (step 6) confirms 'launches renamed Tor binary ugate.exe hidden.' Matching on the literal binary name plus the renamed-Tor heuristic (OriginalFileName=tor.exe under a different image name) is very high fidelity. Corroborated via Microsoft blog, The Hacker News, CyberInsider. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/microsoft-details-windows-clipper.html • https://cyberinsider.com/microsoft-warns-of-usb-worm-like-malware-using-tor-for-stealth/
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user legitimately running Tor renamed to ugate.exe (very unlikely in a managed fleet)
  • Security research/red-team Tor tooling on a sanctioned host
  • An unrelated app coincidentally named ugate.exe with no Tor metadata (excluded by the OriginalFileName check)
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "\\Tor Browser\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the binary's signing/metadata (OriginalFileName/ProductName = Tor) and capture SHA256, parent process, and FolderPath; check whether the parent is a wscript/cscript stealer task. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill ugate.exe, block its hash org-wide, and block 127.0.0.1:9050 / Tor egress. 3) Hunt: search the org for the same SHA256 and for localhost:9050 connections; review clipboard/crypto-wallet usage on the host for substituted addresses.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "ugate.exe"
    or (ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "tor.exe" and FileName !in~ ("tor.exe","firefox.exe"))   // renamed Tor binary
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, OriginalName = ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName, ProductName = ProcessVersionInfoProductName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\ugate.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Renamed Tor Binary ugate.exe Execution (Crypto-Clipper C2)

status: experimental
description: Detects execution of ugate.exe (a renamed Tor binary) or any image whose original filename is tor.exe but runs under another name, used by the crypto-clipper worm for Tor-based C2.

Non-browser process connecting to local Tor SOCKS proxy 127.0.0.1:9050 AICommand & Control High
The stealer routes C2 and exfil through a local Tor SOCKS proxy on localhost:9050 — explicitly called out as a red flag. Hunts loopback connections to TCP 9050 from any process other than a legitimate Tor Browser, surfacing the initiating binary (stealer script host, curl, ugate). Rationale: Article verbatim: 'connections to localhost:9050 and Tor proxy activity are red flags associated with this campaign.' Loopback 9050 from a non-Tor-Browser process is high-signal and EDR-observable. Sentinel left empty because loopback Tor SOCKS connections are an endpoint-only signal not present in this tenant's network/firewall tables (see rationale). Corroborated via Microsoft blog and decoded diagram. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/ • https://www.bleepstatic.com/images/news/u/1220909/2026/June/executionflow.jpg
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer using a standalone Tor SOCKS proxy for testing
  • Privacy tools (qBittorrent/SOCKS-aware apps) pointed at a local Tor service
  • Security team running Tor on a sanctioned research host
  • An app configured with a 9050 proxy that isn't Tor Browser
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Tor Browser\\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tor.exe","obfs4proxy.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — stealer activity shows wscript/cscript/curl or ugate.exe (not a browser) hitting 127.0.0.1:9050; capture cmdline and parent. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the offending process and ugate.exe, and block Tor (9050 + known Tor egress) at the host. 3) Hunt: pivot to ugate.exe execution, curl screenshot exfil, and clipboard/crypto-wallet substitution on the same host; sweep the org for other 9050 loopback talkers.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 9050
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tor.exe","firefox.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "Tor Browser"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 9050
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tor.exe","firefox.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "Tor Browser"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Connection to Local Tor SOCKS Proxy 127.0.0.1:9050 by Non-Browser Process (Crypto-Clipper C2)
id: e7152613-9fa2-4eb0-b132-4d5e6f708192
status: experimental
description: Detects loopback connections to TCP 9050 (Tor SOCKS) from processes other than a legitimate Tor Browser, the C2/exfil channel used by the crypto-clipper worm.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/usb-worm-spreads-crypto-stealing-malware-via-windows-shortcut-files/
author: SOC Detection Engineering

  - Legitimately installed standalone Tor service

#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemotePort=9050 RemoteAddressIP4=/^127\./ | NOT (ContextImageFileName=/(tor|firefox)\.exe$/i) | NOT regex("(?i)Tor Browser", field=ContextImageFileName) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=9050 AND (All_Traffic.dest_ip="127.0.0.1" OR All_Traffic.dest_ip="::1") AND All_Traffic.process_name!="tor.exe" AND All_Traffic.process_name!="firefox.exe" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=9050 AND (All_Traffic.dest_ip="127.0.0.1" OR All_Traffic.dest_ip="::1") AND All_Traffic.process_name!="tor.exe" AND All_Traffic.process_name!="firefox.exe" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Script host executing payload file named 'cfile' (crypto-clipper C2 EVAL RCE) AIActions on Objectives High
The C2 'EVAL' instruction downloads JavaScript into a file named cfile and executes it on the host. Hunts wscript/cscript (or node) executing a file literally named cfile — a remote-code-execution stage with a distinctive, article-named artifact. Rationale: Article: the C2 'EVAL instruction... downloads JavaScript content into a file named cfile, and executes it.' The literal artifact name 'cfile' run by a JS-capable script host is a precise, low-FP RCE indicator. Corroborated against the Microsoft blog (RCE/EVAL described) and diagram step 9. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/microsoft-details-windows-clipper.html
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A build/config script whose path or argument happens to contain 'cfile'
  • Internal tooling that names a config artifact cfile
  • Backup scripts referencing a *.cfile data file
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has ".cfile" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Program Files\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the cmdline and the cfile contents/hash — confirm it is JavaScript executed by wscript/cscript (not a benign data file); capture parent process. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the script-host tree, quarantine cfile, and block ugate.exe/9050 egress to cut the C2 that delivered it. 3) Hunt: search for other cfile writes/executions across the fleet and correlate with localhost:9050 C2 traffic to scope which hosts received EVAL commands.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","node.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "cfile"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\cscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where CommandLine has "cfile"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Script Host Executing Payload File 'cfile' (Crypto-Clipper EVAL RCE)
id: f8263724-a0b3-4fc1-9243-5e6f70819203
status: experimental
description: Detects wscript/cscript/node executing a file named cfile, the JavaScript payload the crypto-clipper C2 drops and runs via its EVAL instruction.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\node.exe) @CommandLine:(*cfile* OR *CFILE*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/(wscript|cscript|node)\.exe$/i | regex("(?i)\bcfile\b", field=CommandLine) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine], function=count())

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","node.exe") AND Processes.process="*cfile*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","node.exe") AND Processes.process="*cfile*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
curl spawned by script host exfiltrating over Tor SOCKS (crypto-clipper screenshot upload) AIActions on Objectives Medium
The stealer captures five screenshots every ten seconds and uploads them to C2 using curl over the Tor SOCKS proxy. Hunts curl.exe launched by a Windows script host with a SOCKS/9050/.onion or file-upload command line — the exfil channel. Rationale: Article: 'the malware also captures five screenshots... every ten seconds and sends them to the C2 using the curl tool,' routed over Tor (localhost:9050). curl as a child of a script host with a SOCKS/9050/.onion or upload flag is article-specific exfil. Corroborated via Microsoft blog and The Hacker News. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/microsoft-details-windows-clipper.html
ATT&CKT1567 T1113
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DevOps scripts using curl --upload-file to an internal artifact store via a proxy
  • CI/automation invoking curl from cmd/powershell with -T
  • Monitoring agents uploading diagnostics through a SOCKS proxy
  • Admin one-off curl upload from a script
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "\\Program Files\\" and ProcessCommandLine !has "://artifactory" and ProcessCommandLine !has "://nexus"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the curl cmdline for the upload target (.onion / 127.0.0.1:9050) and the source file (screenshot .png/.jpg in a temp/staging dir); confirm the parent is a stealer script host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the curl/script-host/ugate tree, block Tor egress, and preserve the staged screenshots for IR. 3) Hunt: look for the repeating 5-screenshots-per-10s capture cadence and other curl→9050 uploads across the fleet; correlate with clipboard wallet-address substitution to confirm active theft.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "curl.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("9050","socks","--socks5","--socks5-hostname","127.0.0.1","localhost",".onion","--upload-file","-T ")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\curl.exe"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\wscript.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\cscript.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("9050","socks","127.0.0.1","localhost",".onion","--upload-file","-T ")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: curl Exfiltration over Tor SOCKS by Script Host (Crypto-Clipper Screenshot Upload)

status: experimental

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/curl\.exe$/i ParentBaseFileName=/(wscript|cscript|powershell|cmd|mshta)\.exe$/i | regex("(?i)(9050|socks|\.onion|--upload-file|-T )", field=CommandLine) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine], function=count())

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="curl.exe" AND Processes.parent_process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe") AND Processes.process IN ("*9050*","*socks*","*127.0.0.1*","*.onion*","*--upload-file*","*-T *") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="curl.exe" AND Processes.parent_process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe") AND Processes.process IN ("*9050*","*socks*","*127.0.0.1*","*.onion*","*--upload-file*","*-T *") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)

Vulnerable googleapis/mcp-toolbox (< 1.4.0) — CVE-2026-11718 opaque-token auth bypass present AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces any managed host whose vulnerability feed reports CVE-2026-11717 / CVE-2026-11718 against the googleapis/mcp-toolbox Go package. This hunts the specific auth-bypass advisory (validateOpaqueToken accepting introspection responses that omit the mandatory RFC 7662 "active" field), not a generic missing-patch query — it anchors on the exact CVE IDs and the mcp-toolbox software name. Rationale: Anchors on the article's two concrete identifiers (CVE-2026-11717/11718) and the affected package name github.com/googleapis/mcp-toolbox; deterministic CVE-feed match, so FP is limited to stale-inventory rather than behavioural noise. Cross-checked the GHSA against CyberPress, CyberSecurityNews and the upstream GitHub issue #3076 which confirm fix version 1.4.0 and CVSS 4.0 9.3. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcpr-6g7x-p44r • https://github.com/googleapis/mcp-toolbox/issues/3076 • https://cyberpress.org/mcp-toolbox-vulnerability-exposed/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/mcp-toolbox-vulnerability/ • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-11718
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host already upgraded to 1.4.0+ but the TVM/scanner snapshot is stale and a re-scan is still pending
  • CVE feed maps the Go module under a SoftwareName that doesn't contain 'toolbox' (vendor naming drift), so a real device is missed rather than false-positive
  • Isolated dev/CI box intentionally pinned to an old version inside a non-routable network
  • Vendored / build-artifact copy of the module flagged as 'installed' though no toolbox service is actually listening
  • Container image scanned by the feed though the image is ephemeral and already destroyed
Suppression filter
| join kind=inner (DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory | where Timestamp > ago(1d) | where SoftwareName has_any ("mcp-toolbox","toolbox") | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId | extend CleanVer = trim_start(@"[vV]", SoftwareVersion) | where CleanVer matches regex @"^\d+(\.\d+)+" | where parse_version(CleanVer) < parse_version("1.4.0")) on DeviceId
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For each dest/DeviceName, confirm a mcp-toolbox process is actually listening (default port 5000) and note whether it's internet-facing; pull SoftwareVersion to verify it is genuinely < 1.4.0 and not a stale record. 2) CONTAIN: Patch to >= 1.4.0 (the fixed release); if patching is delayed, restrict the toolbox's network exposure to trusted clients and verify the configured OAuth introspection endpoint is a trusted, RFC 7662-compliant server that always returns the 'active' field. 3) HUNT: Review toolbox/auth access logs for tool invocations that succeeded against an introspection response lacking 'active', and check for the sibling advisories on the same hosts (CVE-2026-9739 SSE DNS-rebinding, and the issuer-field bypass variant).
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-11717", "CVE-2026-11718")
| where SoftwareVendor has "google" or SoftwareName has_any ("mcp-toolbox", "toolbox")
| summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId, CveId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| sort by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-11717", "CVE-2026-11718")
| where SoftwareVendor has "google" or SoftwareName has_any ("mcp-toolbox", "toolbox")
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceId, CveId
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| sort by DeviceName asc

Internet-facing host running vulnerable mcp-toolbox (< 1.4.0) — exposed auth-bypass surface AIExploitation Medium
Prioritises CVE-2026-11718 exposure by cross-referencing the mcp-toolbox software inventory (version < 1.4.0, the fixed release) against assets flagged internet-facing. Targets the externally reachable instances where an attacker-influenced or non-compliant introspection endpoint could trigger the validateOpaqueToken bypass — a different pivot (inventory + exposure join) than the raw CVE-feed match. Rationale: Uses the article's fixed-version boundary (1.4.0) for an explicit parse_version comparison and the package name, then joins DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing to rank externally exposed instances — the highest-risk targets for a remote token-validation bypass (T1190). Sentinel lacks the DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory table, so the Sentinel variant expresses the same intent via the CVE feed joined to internet-facing assets. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcpr-6g7x-p44r • https://cyberpress.org/mcp-toolbox-vulnerability-exposed/ • https://github.com/googleapis/mcp-toolbox/issues/3076
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SoftwareVersion carries a pre-release/build suffix (e.g. '1.4.0-rc1') that passes the regex but is functionally patched
  • IsInternetFacing flag is stale — host has since been moved behind a firewall or load balancer
  • mcp-toolbox present only as a transitive SDK/library, not the exposed listening server
  • Reverse proxy / WAF fronts the toolbox so the flagged host is exposed but the toolbox port is not actually reachable
  • Inventory shows old version string cached after an in-place binary swap to 1.4.0
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion !startswith "1.4." and SoftwareVersion !startswith "v1.4."
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the toolbox listener is reachable from the public IP (probe the configured port, default 5000) and that SoftwareVersion is genuinely < 1.4.0; validate the OAuth introspection endpoint it trusts is RFC 7662-compliant and always emits 'active'. 2) CONTAIN: Take the external exposure offline or front it with auth-enforcing proxy; upgrade to >= 1.4.0. 3) HUNT: Pull the toolbox/auth logs for the exposure window and look for tool-invocation successes tied to introspection responses missing 'active', plus the related SSE DNS-rebinding (CVE-2026-9739) and issuer-omission bypass on the same internet-facing fleet.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareName has_any ("mcp-toolbox", "toolbox") and SoftwareVendor has "google"
| extend CleanVer = trim_start(@"[vV]", SoftwareVersion)
| where CleanVer matches regex @"^\d+(\.\d+)+"
| where parse_version(CleanVer) < parse_version("1.4.0")
| summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId, SoftwareName
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d) | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| where IsInternetFacing == true
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP
| sort by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-11717", "CVE-2026-11718")
| where SoftwareVendor has "google" or SoftwareName has_any ("mcp-toolbox", "toolbox")
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceId
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d) | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| where IsInternetFacing == true
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP
| sort by DeviceName asc

Kirby Panel install surface accessed on a live site (CVE-2026-54003) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts any HTTP request to the Kirby Panel installation routes (/panel/installation or /api/system/install) on a production site. An already-initialised Kirby install never legitimately serves these routes, so traffic here on a live site indicates external-initialization probing or exploitation of CVE-2026-54003 via the spoofable Forwarded/X-Client-IP/X-Real-IP headers. Rationale: Uses the exact Kirby install routes /panel/installation and /api/system/install named in the advisory and confirmed in Kirby docs; on a live site any non-404/403 hit is anomalous. Client-IP filtering is deliberately omitted because behind a reverse proxy the logged cIP is the proxy, not the attacker (the spoofed IP lives in the Forwarded/X-Real-IP header). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-whxw-24jc-cwmv • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/getkirby/cms/CVE-2026-54003/ • https://github.com/getkirby/kirby/releases/tag/5.4.4
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internet background scanners probing common CMS/admin paths like /panel
  • Legitimate first-time deployment of a brand-new Kirby site within the maintenance window
  • Authorized vulnerability scanning or pentest engagement against the site
  • Synthetic uptime/availability monitors crawling Panel routes
  • Staging/dev Kirby instance shipping access logs into the same workspace
Suppression filter
| where toint(scStatus) !in (404, 403)
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull all install-route hits; check the response code and whether this host is a brand-new deploy (no admin yet) versus an established site. Cross-reference proxy logs for the Forwarded/X-Client-IP/X-Real-IP header and the true client IP. 2) Contain: If the site was already live, treat as compromise — set 'api'=>false or take Panel offline, and update Kirby to 4.9.4/5.4.4. 3) Hunt: Pivot to UC 'admin account created' to see if a POST succeeded, then review Panel logins, new users, and uploaded templates/plugins for webshells.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem has "/panel/installation" or csUriStem has "/api/system/install"
| where toint(scStatus) !in (404, 403)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
