Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Salesforce sObject enumeration recon (/services/data/v59.0/sobjects mapping)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Salesforce REST API access from Icarus/Klue-breach IPs (138.226.246.94 et al.)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Salesforce bulk /query exfiltration burst via abused Klue OAuth token · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Salesforce REST API access from Icarus/Klue-breach IPs (138.226.246.94 et al.) AIExploitation High
Hunts any Salesforce API or SaaS-connector activity sourced from the four IP addresses ReliaQuest and Huntress attributed to the Icarus actor's OAuth-token abuse against Klue Battlecards customers. Because access used valid stolen OAuth tokens, the source IP is the highest-fidelity differentiator between the attacker and the legitimate Klue integration. Rationale: Anchored on the four IPs jointly published by ReliaQuest and Huntress (two-source confirmed) plus the article's exact Salesforce REST API base path `/services/data/`. IP + Salesforce-app scope is a hard IOC with near-zero legitimate overlap. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-integration-abused-in-crm-data-theft/ • https://www.huntress.com/blog/klue-breach-investigation • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/salesforce-disables-klue-app.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/19/klue-salesforce-data-breach-huntress/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1078.004
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A corporate user genuinely behind a shared egress NAT that coincidentally overlaps one of the listed IPs (verify ownership/ASN first)
  • Threat-intel scanning or a SOC validation test deliberately replaying the IOC IPs against the tenant
  • A VPN/proxy provider re-allocating one of these IPs to a benign customer weeks after the campaign
  • Security vendor (ReliaQuest/Huntress) re-accessing the tenant during incident response from related infrastructure
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the Salesforce ConnectedApp / OAuth token tied to the hits is the Klue Battlecards integration and pull the AccountObjectId + token ID; check whether the IP's ASN belongs to a hosting/VPN provider. 2) Contain: immediately revoke and rotate the Klue Battlecards OAuth tokens, terminate active Salesforce API sessions for that connected app, and block the four IPs at the CASB/proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same token/connected-app to enumerate every sObject queried and record volume pulled (UC: bulk /query burst), and check HubSpot, SharePoint, Zoom, Gong, Chorus, Clari, Google Drive and Slack — the other integrations Klue disabled — for activity from the same IPs.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| where IPAddress in ("138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160")
| summarize EventCount = count(), Actions = make_set(ActionType, 20), Objects = make_set(ObjectType, 20), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ISP, CountryCode, UserAgent
| order by EventCount desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| where IPAddress in ("138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160")
| summarize EventCount = count(), Actions = make_set(ActionType, 20), Objects = make_set(ObjectType, 20), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ISP, CountryCode, UserAgent
| order by EventCount desc
title: Salesforce API Access From Icarus Klue-Breach IP Addresses
id: 6f1a9c4e-2d3b-4f7a-9c1e-8b2d5a0f1c34
description: Detects Salesforce REST API requests originating from IP addresses attributed by ReliaQuest and Huntress to the Icarus actor's OAuth-token theft against Klue Battlecards customers.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/klue-oauth-breach-linked-to-icarus-salesforce-data-theft-attacks/
  - https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-integration-abused-in-crm-data-theft/
  - https://www.huntress.com/blog/klue-breach-investigation
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:
  - attack.t1550.001
  - attack.t1078.004
logsource:
  category: proxy
detection:
  selection:
    c-ip:
      - '138.226.246.94'
      - '212.86.125.24'
      - '213.111.148.90'
      - '94.154.32.160'
    cs-uri-stem|contains: '/services/data/'
  condition: selection
level: high
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(Web.url) as urls, values(Web.http_method) as methods from datamodel=Web where Web.src IN ("138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160") AND Web.url="*/services/data/*" by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.user, Web.dest_zone | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(Web.url) as urls, values(Web.http_method) as methods from datamodel=Web where Web.src IN ("138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160") AND Web.url="*/services/data/*" by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.user, Web.dest_zone | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - count
Salesforce bulk /query exfiltration burst via abused Klue OAuth token AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the high-volume exfiltration stage where the Icarus actor sent close to a thousand calls to the Salesforce `/services/data/v59.0/query` REST endpoint inside a ~15-minute window (and a separate 6-hour pull) using a stolen Klue OAuth token. Targets the volumetric burst that traded stealth for speed once valuable objects were identified. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact endpoint `/services/data/v59.0/query` and the documented ~1000-calls-in-15-minutes burst rate; counting calls per source per 15-min bin reproduces the 'burst traded stealth for speed' behaviour ReliaQuest described. Threshold is volumetric not signature, hence hunting tier. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-integration-abused-in-crm-data-theft/ • https://www.huntress.com/blog/klue-breach-investigation • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/salesforce-disables-klue-app.html
ATT&CKT1567 T1213
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Klue Battlecards (or another sanctioned ETL/BI connector) running a scheduled full-CRM sync that legitimately exceeds the call threshold
  • Salesforce Data Loader / dataloader.io bulk export run by a sales-ops admin
  • A backup or DLP product performing a periodic mass read of CRM objects
  • Marketing-automation integration (e.g. a CDP) doing an initial historical backfill
Suppression filter
// Suppress sanctioned high-volume connectors once their service-account ObjectIds/IPs are baselined:
| where IPAddress !in ("<your_sanctioned_etl_egress_ips_are_not_known_here>")  // NOTE: leave this clause out unless you maintain an allowlist; better to whitelist by verified AccountObjectId in the summarize step
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the OAuth ConnectedApp and AccountObjectId behind the burst and confirm whether it is the Klue Battlecards token; check the source IP against the four Icarus IOCs. 2) Contain: revoke/rotate the implicated OAuth token, kill active API sessions, and temporarily throttle or disable the connected app if it is not a verified business sync. 3) Hunt: reconstruct which sObjects were pulled (CRM contacts, quotes, competitive-intel reports per Huntress) to scope the data loss, and look back for the slow `/services/data/v59.0/sobjects` enumeration that preceded the burst.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| summarize ApiActivityCount = count(), DistinctObjects = dcount(ObjectName), SampleAction = any(ActionType), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, bin(Timestamp, 15m)
| where ApiActivityCount > 200   // ReliaQuest: ~1000 /query calls in a single 15-min burst; 200 = conservative alert floor
| order by ApiActivityCount desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| summarize ApiActivityCount = count(), DistinctObjects = dcount(ObjectName), SampleAction = any(ActionType), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 15m)
| where ApiActivityCount > 200   // ReliaQuest: ~1000 /query calls in a single 15-min burst; 200 = conservative alert floor
| order by ApiActivityCount desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count as QueryCalls, dc(Web.uri_query) as DistinctQueries, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/services/data/v59.0/query*" by Web.src, Web.user, _time span=15m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where QueryCalls > 200 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - QueryCalls
| tstats summariesonly=false count as QueryCalls, dc(Web.uri_query) as DistinctQueries, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/services/data/v59.0/query*" by Web.src, Web.user, _time span=15m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where QueryCalls > 200 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - QueryCalls
Salesforce sObject enumeration recon (/services/data/v59.0/sobjects mapping) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts the slow reconnaissance stage where the Icarus actor methodically enumerated a Salesforce org's objects via the `/services/data/v59.0/sobjects` endpoint to map out which objects held valuable data before exfiltrating. Surfaces a single token/IP touching an unusually wide set of distinct sObjects over a steady, low-and-slow window. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact recon endpoint `/services/data/v59.0/sobjects` and the described behaviour of 'slowly mapped out their Salesforce objects to identify valuable objects'; counting distinct objects/types touched per source per hour captures the enumeration without depending on a fixed signature. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-integration-abused-in-crm-data-theft/ • https://www.huntress.com/blog/klue-breach-investigation
ATT&CKT1526 T1213
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A newly installed integration performing its first-run schema discovery (legitimately walks every sObject once)
  • A Salesforce admin or developer running a metadata/schema audit tool (e.g. Workbench, sfdx) against the org
  • A data-catalog or governance product profiling object metadata
  • QA/sandbox refresh tooling enumerating object definitions
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the enumerating token is a brand-new or recently-modified connected app vs an established one, and whether the source IP matches the four Icarus IOCs. 2) Contain: if the app/token is not a recognized first-run integration, revoke the OAuth token and suspend the connected app pending review. 3) Hunt: check whether the same token transitioned from this slow `/sobjects` enumeration into a bulk `/services/data/v59.0/query` burst (the exfiltration UC) — that recon→exfil sequence on one token is the strong confirmation of the Icarus pattern.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| summarize DistinctObjectTypes = dcount(ObjectType), ObjectSample = make_set(ObjectType, 50), TotalReads = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where DistinctObjectTypes > 25   // wide object enumeration = mapping the org before targeted theft
| order by DistinctObjectTypes desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| summarize DistinctObjectTypes = dcount(ObjectType), ObjectSample = make_set(ObjectType, 50), TotalReads = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctObjectTypes > 25   // wide object enumeration = mapping the org before targeted theft
| order by DistinctObjectTypes desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count, dc(Web.uri_path) as DistinctObjectPaths, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/services/data/v59.0/sobjects*" by Web.src, Web.user, _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where DistinctObjectPaths > 25 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - DistinctObjectPaths
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Web.uri_path) as DistinctObjectPaths, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/services/data/v59.0/sobjects*" by Web.src, Web.user, _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where DistinctObjectPaths > 25 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - DistinctObjectPaths
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |
    User-driven consent to a third-party OAuth application — illicit-
    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic
    in your SIEM for higher fidelity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1528
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate first-time SaaS app onboarding
level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] INC Veeam backup credential dumping (salted DPAPI SQL secret access) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — INC Ransomware Emerges as Major RaaS Threat in 2026 with 830+ Victims Since 2023
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] INC Ransomware BYOVD vulnerable driver drop (filwfp.sys / filnk.sys / fildds.sys) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] INC Rust encryptor launched with --esxi hypervisor argument · [LLM] INC Ransomware Rclone cloud exfiltration of staged archives · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
INC Ransomware BYOVD vulnerable driver drop (filwfp.sys / filnk.sys / fildds.sys) AIInstallation High
Hunts the file write or load of the three named vulnerable kernel drivers INC ransomware affiliates use to blind EDR/AV before encryption. These filenames are not legitimate Windows or vendor drivers, so any appearance is high-fidelity; Sophos observed all three loaded onto one network within seven minutes. Rationale: Uses the three exact BYOVD driver filenames from the article, independently confirmed by Sophos X-Ops (three loads in 7 minutes on one network). No legitimate driver carries these names, so a bare file-create match is high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://x.com/SophosXOps/status/1764933957286855058 • https://www.acronis.com/en/tru/posts/from-emerging-threat-to-top-tier-ransomware-as-a-service-the-evolution-of-inc-ransomware/ • https://www.picussecurity.com/resource/blog/what-are-bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver-byovd-attacks
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1068 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher detonating INC samples in a sanctioned malware lab
  • EDR/AV vendor signature test files staged under a quarantine folder
  • Threat-intel team copying captured driver samples to a forensic share
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\ProgramData\\Microsoft\\Windows Defender" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Sandbox\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess that wrote the .sys file and whether the host is a backup/edge server; check for a same-host service-create or driver-load event seconds later. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately and block the driver hash org-wide; INC drops these only minutes before mass encryption. 3) Hunt: pivot on the writing process tree for prior Veeam credential access, rclone exfil, and RMM (AnyDesk/ScreenConnect/TeamViewer) installs across the estate.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("filwfp.sys", "filnk.sys", "fildds.sys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp asc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("filwfp.sys", "filnk.sys", "fildds.sys")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DvcAction, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName,
          ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated asc
title: INC Ransomware BYOVD Vulnerable Driver Drop (filwfp/filnk/fildds.sys)
id: 6d2f1a44-9c1e-4f7b-8a3d-1b9c2e5a7f01
description: Detects creation of the vulnerable kernel drivers filwfp.sys, filnk.sys and fildds.sys used by INC ransomware affiliates for BYOVD defense impairment.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/inc-ransomware-claims-830-victims-since.html
  - https://x.com/SophosXOps/status/1764933957286855058
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:
  - attack.t1562.001
  - attack.t1068
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\filwfp.sys'
      - '\filnk.sys'
      - '\fildds.sys'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Extremely unlikely; these filenames are not shipped by Microsoft or legitimate vendors.
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\filwfp.sys OR *\\filnk.sys OR *\\fildds.sys OR *\\FILWFP.SYS OR *\\FILNK.SYS OR *\\FILDDS.SYS OR *\\Filwfp.sys OR *\\Filnk.sys OR *\\Fildds.sys)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\\(filwfp|filnk|fildds)\.sys$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action=created (Filesystem.file_name="filwfp.sys" OR Filesystem.file_name="filnk.sys" OR Filesystem.file_name="fildds.sys") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_id Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action=created (Filesystem.file_name="filwfp.sys" OR Filesystem.file_name="filnk.sys" OR Filesystem.file_name="fildds.sys") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_id Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
INC Rust encryptor launched with --esxi hypervisor argument AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts execution of a process invoked with INC ransomware's documented '--esxi' command-line flag, which triggers the Rust encryptor to shut down running virtual machines before encrypting ESXi datastores. Targets Linux/ESXi hosts where Defender for Endpoint or auditd telemetry is available. Rationale: The '--esxi' operator flag that drives the encryptor to power off VMs is stated verbatim in the article and corroborated by Acronis/CybersecurityNews reporting on the Rust Linux/ESXi variant. It is an unusual token rarely seen in benign command lines. Cross-checked against: • https://www.acronis.com/en/tru/posts/from-emerging-threat-to-top-tier-ransomware-as-a-service-the-evolution-of-inc-ransomware/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/inc-ransomware-uses-rust-based-windows/amp/ • https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/inc-ransomware-thrives-by-mastering-the-basics
ATT&CKT1486 T1529
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin VM-migration or DR scripts that pass an --esxi parameter to an internal tool
  • Backup/replication jobs invoking ESXi automation with a similar flag
  • Security testing of ESXi-targeting tooling in a lab cluster
Suppression filter
| where not(FolderPath has_any ("/usr/lib/vmware", "/opt/vmware")) and FileName !in~ ("vim-cmd", "esxcli", "vmware-vim-cmd")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the binary is unsigned/unknown and not a sanctioned VMware utility; check the host for simultaneous mass VM power-off (vim-cmd / esxcli vm process kill). 2) Contain: power-isolate the ESXi host from management/storage networks and snapshot datastores if not yet encrypted. 3) Hunt: review the host for the BYOVD driver drops, rclone exfil, and lateral RDP/PsExec inbound from the same operator account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--esxi"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp asc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "--esxi" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "--esxi"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName,
          TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated asc
title: INC Ransomware Encryptor ESXi VM-Shutdown Argument
id: a1f4c9b2-7e83-4d61-9c0a-2f5b8d3e6c12
description: Detects a process launched with INC ransomware's --esxi flag, which shuts down VMs prior to hypervisor encryption.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/inc-ransomware-claims-830-victims-since.html
  - https://www.acronis.com/en/tru/posts/from-emerging-threat-to-top-tier-ransomware-as-a-service-the-evolution-of-inc-ransomware/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:
  - attack.t1486
  - attack.t1529
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    CommandLine|contains: '--esxi'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate VMware/ESXi tooling or scripts that accept an --esxi switch.
level: medium
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:*--esxi*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| CommandLine=/--esxi/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*--esxi*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*--esxi*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
INC Ransomware Rclone cloud exfiltration of staged archives AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts INC's data-theft step: rclone (or a renamed rclone identified by its characteristic flags) copying/syncing data to an external cloud remote after the operator stages it as password-protected archives. Catches both the named binary and renamed copies via flag fingerprinting. Rationale: Rclone is the exfiltration tool named in the article; the renamed-binary fallback fingerprints rclone's distinctive --config/--transfers/--multi-thread-streams flags so a rename to evade the binary-name match still fires. Pairs with the article's password-protected-archive staging (T1560.001). Cross-checked against: • https://www.acronis.com/en/tru/posts/from-emerging-threat-to-top-tier-ransomware-as-a-service-the-evolution-of-inc-ransomware/ • https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/inc-ransomware-thrives-by-mastering-the-basics
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1560.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT/backup teams using rclone for legitimate cloud backup or migration
  • DevOps syncing artifacts to S3/B2/GDrive via rclone in CI
  • Personal-use rclone on a developer workstation copying to a cloud remote
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe", "backup-agent.exe") and AccountName !startswith "svc-backup"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the rclone command line for the remote target and source path; cloud destinations (mega/b2/onedrive) sourcing from file shares or backup volumes are high risk. 2) Contain: block the destination domain/IP at egress, suspend the executing account, and preserve the rclone config (often holds the attacker's remote creds). 3) Hunt: look for 7-Zip/WinRAR/rar processes creating password-protected (-p/-hp) archives on the same host just before, and correlate with BYOVD driver drops signalling imminent encryption.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "rclone.exe"
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--config"
       and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--transfers", "--multi-thread-streams", "--no-check-certificate", "--ignore-existing")
       and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("copy", "sync", "move"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp asc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\rclone.exe"
   or (CommandLine has "--config"
       and (CommandLine has "--transfers" or CommandLine has "--multi-thread-streams" or CommandLine has "--no-check-certificate")
       and (CommandLine has "copy" or CommandLine has "sync" or CommandLine has "move"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated asc
title: INC Ransomware Rclone Cloud Exfiltration
id: c7b9e1d3-4a2f-4e88-bd51-9a6c0f2b8e34
description: Detects rclone execution used by INC ransomware affiliates to exfiltrate staged archives to cloud storage.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/inc-ransomware-claims-830-victims-since.html
  - https://www.acronis.com/en/tru/posts/from-emerging-threat-to-top-tier-ransomware-as-a-service-the-evolution-of-inc-ransomware/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:
  - attack.t1567.002
  - attack.t1560.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith: '\rclone.exe'
  selection_flags:
    CommandLine|contains: '--config'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '--transfers'
      - '--multi-thread-streams'
      - '--no-check-certificate'
  condition: selection_img or selection_flags
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate rclone backup or sync jobs run by IT/backup teams.
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*\\rclone.exe OR *\\Rclone.exe OR *\\RCLONE.EXE) OR (@CommandLine:*--config* AND (@CommandLine:*--transfers* OR @CommandLine:*--multi-thread-streams* OR @CommandLine:*--no-check-certificate*) AND (@CommandLine:*copy* OR @CommandLine:*sync* OR @CommandLine:*move*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\rclone\.exe$/i OR (CommandLine=/--config/i AND CommandLine=/(--transfers|--multi-thread-streams|--no-check-certificate)/i AND CommandLine=/(copy|sync|move)/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="rclone.exe") OR (Processes.process="*--config*" AND (Processes.process="*--transfers*" OR Processes.process="*--multi-thread-streams*" OR Processes.process="*--no-check-certificate*") AND (Processes.process="*copy*" OR Processes.process="*sync*" OR Processes.process="*move*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="rclone.exe") OR (Processes.process="*--config*" AND (Processes.process="*--transfers*" OR Processes.process="*--multi-thread-streams*" OR Processes.process="*--no-check-certificate*") AND (Processes.process="*copy*" OR Processes.process="*sync*" OR Processes.process="*move*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
INC Veeam backup credential dumping (salted DPAPI SQL secret access) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts INC's updated credential dumper reading Veeam Backup & Replication's stored SQL credentials (SqlLogin / SqlSecuredPassword DPAPI blobs) or the VeeamBackup Credentials table from a non-Veeam process on a backup server. Targets the credential-access step that lets INC neutralize recovery before encryption. Rationale: Anchors on Veeam's real credential-store internals — the SqlLogin/SqlSecuredPassword DPAPI registry values under 'Veeam Backup and Replication' and the VeeamBackup [Credentials] table — which the article's salted-DPAPI Veeam dumper must touch; the non-Veeam-parent filter keeps it focused on the attacker tool, not the product itself. Cross-checked against: • https://www.acronis.com/en/tru/posts/from-emerging-threat-to-top-tier-ransomware-as-a-service-the-evolution-of-inc-ransomware/ • https://securitybrief.com.au/story/inc-ransomware-surges-as-australia-stays-in-sights
ATT&CKT1003 T1555 T1552.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam admins running official credential-migration or upgrade scripts
  • Backup-monitoring tooling querying the VeeamBackup config DB
  • DBA running ad-hoc SELECTs against the VeeamBackup database during troubleshooting
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("veeamadmin", "svc-veeam") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sqlservr.exe", "postgres.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the executing binary/account is not a sanctioned Veeam component or admin; review whether it ran on a designated backup server. 2) Contain: rotate all credentials stored in Veeam (service, repository, vCenter/ESXi, cloud) and isolate the backup server, since dumped creds enable backup deletion and lateral movement. 3) Hunt: trace the operator account to inbound RDP/RMM sessions, look for backup-job or repository deletion, and the BYOVD driver drops that precede INC encryption.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "Veeam Backup and Replication" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("SqlSecuredPassword", "SqlLogin"))
     or (ProcessCommandLine has "VeeamBackup" and ProcessCommandLine has "Credentials")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Veeam.Backup.Manager.exe", "Veeam.Backup.Service.exe", "Veeam.Backup.PowerShell.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp asc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetProcessCommandLine has "Veeam Backup and Replication" and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("SqlSecuredPassword", "SqlLogin"))
     or (TargetProcessCommandLine has "VeeamBackup" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "Credentials")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("Veeam.Backup.Manager.exe", "Veeam.Backup.Service.exe", "Veeam.Backup.PowerShell.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName,
          TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated asc
title: INC Ransomware Veeam Credential Store Access
id: e2a8d5f6-1c47-4b39-8e02-7d4a9c1f3b56
description: Detects non-Veeam processes reading Veeam Backup & Replication stored SQL credentials or the VeeamBackup Credentials table, matching INC's Veeam DPAPI credential dumper.

  - https://www.acronis.com/en/tru/posts/from-emerging-threat-to-top-tier-ransomware-as-a-service-the-evolution-of-inc-ransomware/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:

logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_reg:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'Veeam Backup and Replication'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'SqlSecuredPassword'
      - 'SqlLogin'
  selection_db:

falsepositives:

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents

         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;

    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"

              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental

references:

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PraisonAI UI (aiui) server spawns shell/LOLBin child via unauth MCP connect RCE AIExploitation High
Hunts the post-exploitation execution step of GHSA-p75f-6fp4-p57w: the PraisonAI UI host app (launched via `aiui run` / `praisonai ui` / `praisonai claw`) starting an attacker-chosen local process through the MCP stdio transport. Legitimate MCP stdio servers are npx/uvx/node/python runtimes; a raw shell, touch, curl, wget or nc child of the aiui server is the RCE signature. Rationale: Pivots on the article's exact server-launch strings (`aiui run`, `praisonai ui`, `praisonai claw` from ui.py/claw.py) as the parent and a raw shell/LOLBin child — no legitimate MCP stdio server is a bare shell. Datadog left empty because linux.auditd EXECVE in this tenant exposes no parent-process field to anchor the aiui pivot. Falcon limited to ParentBaseFileName since FDR ProcessRollup2 carries no parent command line. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p75f-6fp4-p57w • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/npm/mcp-bridge/GHSA-wvr4-3wq4-gpc5/ • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation • https://github.com/MervinPraison/PraisonAI/security/advisories/GHSA-9qhq-v63v-fv3j
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-configured MCP server whose stdio command is a shell wrapper script (e.g. a `bash -c` launcher around a real MCP binary)
  • Admin/SRE debugging the aiui service from the same process tree (interactive shell under the service)
  • An MCP server config that uses curl/wget to fetch from a package registry on startup
  • Health-check or readiness probe scripts shelling out under the service account
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("registry.npmjs.org","pypi.org","ghcr.io","objects.githubusercontent.com"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ChildCmd and ParentCmd — confirm the child is a real shell/exfil tool, not an MCP runtime, and check whether the aiui service is internet-exposed (bound 0.0.0.0). 2) Contain: kill the child PID, isolate/cordon the host, and immediately set `AUTH_ENFORCE=true` (or take the UI offline) so /api/mcp/connect is no longer unauthenticated; rotate any secrets readable by the UI service user. 3) Hunt: review proxy/web logs for prior POSTs to /api/mcp/connect, enumerate sibling children of the aiui process, and check for follow-on persistence (cron, systemd units, SSH keys) written by the same account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("aiui run","praisonai ui","praisonai claw","create_host_app","build_host_app") or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "aiui"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","fish","busybox","touch","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","chmod","base64","whoami","id","uname","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| where not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("registry.npmjs.org","pypi.org","ghcr.io","objects.githubusercontent.com"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("aiui run","praisonai ui","praisonai claw","create_host_app","build_host_app")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/ksh","/fish","busybox","touch","curl","wget","/nc","ncat","socat","chmod","base64","whoami","/id","uname","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage = TargetProcessName, ChildCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unauthenticated POST to PraisonAI /api/mcp/connect MCP endpoint AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to the vulnerable PraisonAIUI route `POST /api/mcp/connect` (and `/api/mcp/servers`) exposed by the UI host app on 0.0.0.0 without auth. Surfaces exploitation attempts at the wire level before code executes, complementing the host-side process detection. Rationale: Uses the article's exact route strings `/api/mcp/connect` and `/api/mcp/servers` (registered at praisonaiui/server.py:2769-2770) plus the POST method from the documented PoC request. Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch empty because the request body and URI live only in proxy/web-access logs, not in EDR or AWS CloudTrail telemetry in this tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p75f-6fp4-p57w • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/npm/mcp-bridge/GHSA-wvr4-3wq4-gpc5/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate operator adding an MCP server through the PraisonAI UI, which issues the same POST /api/mcp/connect from the browser
  • Internal vulnerability scanner or ASM probe hitting the endpoint
  • CI/CD smoke test that exercises the MCP connect route
  • Load balancer / uptime monitor configured to POST to the API path
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the SourceIP — is it external/untrusted or an internal admin workstation? Correlate the timestamp against UC1 process-spawn alerts on the destination host. 2) Contain: if the source is untrusted, block it at the WAF/proxy and restrict the aiui listener to localhost or behind authenticated reverse proxy (set AUTH_ENFORCE=true). 3) Hunt: pull all requests from that SourceIP, look for repeated POSTs (PoC retries until the process wins scheduling) and any subsequent host-side child-process execution.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/api/mcp/connect" or RequestURL has "/api/mcp/servers"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PraisonAI AgentOS unauthenticated POST /api/chat remote agent invocation AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated HTTP requests to the AgentOS FastAPI routes POST /api/chat and GET /api/agents that return 200 with no Authorization header — the exact incomplete-fix surface in CVE-2026-40151. A no-auth 200 on these paths means an external client successfully enumerated or drove the deployed agent (triggering its tools, memory, and cost-bearing model calls). Rationale: Uses the article's exact incomplete-fix routes (POST /api/chat, GET /api/agents) and the documented behaviour that no-auth requests return 200 (vs 401 on the hardened sibling control). HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization empty + 200 is the clean true positive for unauthenticated invocation; corroborated by the GHSA, the CVE-2026-40151 record, and public reports of rapid endpoint scanning. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-892r-p3jq-jp24 • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/cve-2026-40151-cwe-200-exposure-of-sensitive-infor-41548a8f • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-892r-p3jq-jp24 • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation
ATT&CKT1190 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Kubernetes liveness/readiness probes GETting /api/agents (UA kube-probe)
  • Cloud load-balancer health checks (ELB-HealthChecker) hitting the route
  • An upstream API gateway that terminated auth at the edge, so the backend log shows no Authorization header
  • CI/CD smoke tests invoking the deployed agent post-deploy
  • Internal developers calling the API directly on a trusted network where auth was intentionally disabled
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1","::1") and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "kube-probe" and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "ELB-HealthChecker" and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "GoogleHC"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all 200 responses to /api/chat and /api/agents grouped by source IP; confirm whether the caller is external (non-RFC1918, not a known LB/proxy) and whether the Authorization header was absent. Check the AgentOS process owner and what tools/memory the agent wraps. 2) Contain: place the AgentOS listener behind an authenticating reverse proxy or rebind to 127.0.0.1, or block port 8000 at the perimeter immediately; rotate any API keys/secrets the agent had access to. 3) Hunt: review request bodies for /api/chat to identify what messages were sent (data exfiltration, tool abuse), pivot on the source IP across other internet-facing assets, and check for the GET /api/agents enumeration that typically precedes invocation.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/api/chat" or Url has "/api/agents"
| where HttpMethod in~ ("POST","GET")
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)   // no bearer token presented
| where HttpStatusCode == 200                      // vulnerable AgentOS returns 200, a patched/proxied one returns 401
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, UserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

PraisonAI AgentOS process bound to 0.0.0.0:8000 / external inbound connections AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the misconfiguration root cause: a PraisonAI/uvicorn process launched with the default host=0.0.0.0 port=8000 and/or accepting inbound connections from public IPs on 8000. This is the network-exposure precondition that makes the unauthenticated AgentOS routes reachable. Rationale: Anchors on the article's literal config defaults (host="0.0.0.0", port=8000) and the praisonai/AgentOS/AgentApp module names, plus public inbound on 8000. This catches the exposed-listener root cause regardless of whether an exploit request has landed yet — the 0.0.0.0 default is called out as the root cause in the advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-892r-p3jq-jp24 • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/cve-2026-40151-cwe-200-exposure-of-sensitive-infor-41548a8f
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Intentional production deployment with AgentOS on 0.0.0.0 but fronted by an authenticating reverse proxy (the advisory's recommended pattern)
  • Containers binding 0.0.0.0 inside an isolated pod network with no real internet exposure
  • Dev/test instances deliberately reachable on a trusted LAN
  • Public inbound connections that are actually from a known ingress controller / WAF source IP, not real external clients
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIPs !has "10." and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "127.0.0.1"
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit, determine whether the host is genuinely internet-facing (DeviceInfo IsInternetFacing / public IP) and whether an authenticating proxy sits in front of port 8000. 2) Contain: if exposed without auth, rebind AgentOS to 127.0.0.1 or place it behind a bearer-auth proxy and firewall port 8000; treat as exploitable per CVE-2026-40151 since v4.5.128–v4.6.57 and main are all vulnerable. 3) Hunt: cross-reference with web-log UC1 to see if any unauthenticated /api/chat or /api/agents 200s already occurred against this listener, and inventory other hosts running the same praisonai version.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort == 8000
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","python.exe","python3.exe","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","agentos","AgentApp","AgentOS")
| summarize ConnCount=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), RemoteIPs=make_set(RemoteIP, 100) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, LocalPort
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","agentos","AgentApp","AgentOS")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "0.0.0.0" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "8000"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable PraisonAI package inventory (CVE-2026-40151, >= 4.2.1 <= 4.6.57) AIReconnaissance Medium
Surfaces hosts with the praisonai / praisonaiagents package installed in the confirmed-vulnerable range (incl. the supposedly-patched v4.5.128 and latest v4.6.57). Used to scope exposure for the unauthenticated AgentOS incomplete-fix advisory. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE id (CVE-2026-40151) and the advisory's confirmed-affected range (>= 4.2.1, <= 4.6.57 — including the falsely-patched 4.5.128 and latest 4.6.57). This is posture scoping: it tells the SOC which assets need the network-exposure and web-log detections applied. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-892r-p3jq-jp24 • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-892r-p3jq-jp24
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

Response runbook
1) Triage: list all hosts running praisonai/praisonaiagents and join against internet-facing status; prioritize any in the 4.2.1–4.6.57 range that also appear in the UC2 exposed-listener results. 2) Contain: since no fixed release exists yet (main still reproduces), apply compensating controls — bind to 127.0.0.1 or front with an authenticating proxy, and firewall port 8000 — rather than relying on a version bump. 3) Hunt: feed the asset list into UC1/UC2 to detect actual unauthenticated invocation, and monitor the advisory for a real fixed version to drive remediation.

Unauthenticated PraisonAI AgentTeam.launch agent invocation via /agents endpoints AIExploitation Medium
Hunts external HTTP requests that hit PraisonAI's unauthenticated AgentTeam.launch()/Agents.launch() routes: GET /{path}/list (agent enumeration), POST /{path} (sequential team invocation) and POST /{path}/{agent_id} (single-agent invocation), defaulting to /agents. Because the launch path registers no auth middleware, every 200 response is by definition unauthenticated agent execution (GHSA-x8cv-xmq7-p8xp, sibling of CVE-2026-44338 / CVE-2026-40151). Rationale: Anchored on the article's concrete route shapes (GET /{path}/list, POST /{path}, POST /{path}/{agent_id}; default path /agents from the PoC) plus the fact that no Authorization parsing exists in the launch path, so any 200 from a public source IP is unauthenticated agent execution. Corroborated by sibling advisories and observed in-the-wild scanning of /agents and /chat. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation • https://gbhackers.com/praisonai-vulnerability-actively-exploited/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/pypi/praisonai/CVE-2026-39889/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal application/front-end calling its own PraisonAI /agents API from a corporate egress IP that resolves as public
  • Authorized API consumers or partner integrations invoking the agent team intentionally
  • Security scanners / ASM tooling (e.g. internal pentest, Nuclei templates) probing /agents/list
  • Uptime monitors polling the documented /health and adjacent routes
  • DAST pipelines in CI hitting the staging endpoint
Suppression filter
| where UserAgents !has_any ("PraisonAI-internal", "uptime-monitor")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the full request set for the offending CIp — confirm whether /agents/list (enumeration) preceded a POST /agents or POST /agents/{id} (invocation), inspect User-Agent and request bodies for prompt-injection or data-exfil markers, and verify the source IP is not a sanctioned consumer. 2) Contain: Put the PraisonAI launch endpoint behind auth or network ACLs immediately (the launch path ships no token check); block the source IP at the WAF/reverse proxy and, if internet-exposed, take the service off 0.0.0.0. 3) Hunt: Review all historical hits on the route shapes, pivot on the host running the server for outbound connections or tool/agent actions triggered by the injected prompts, and confirm whether the deployment is on a patched/hardened build vs. current main.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ScStatus == 200
| where (CsMethod == "GET" and tolower(CsUriStem) endswith "/agents/list")
     or (CsMethod == "POST" and tolower(CsUriStem) matches regex @"/agents(/[^/]+)?$")
| where not(ipv4_is_private(CIp))
| summarize Requests = count(), Methods = make_set(CsMethod), Paths = make_set(CsUriStem), UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 5), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by CIp, CsHost
| order by Requests desc
